knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
Life_Expectancy_Data <- read.csv("Life-Expectancy-Data-Updated.csv")
```

# Checking data
First, we want to see the structure of our data. What variables do we have, for which countries, etc. 
Then we will check if the data has any empty, missing or weird entries.
Lastly, we will give some Rshiny tools so you can explore the data yourself. 

## Data structure
### What columns do we have? How many rows?
```{r}
colnames(Life_Expectancy_Data)

paste(nrow(Life_Expectancy_Data), "rows")
```
There are 21 columns and 2864 rows. 
Important to note for some columns:  
* Hepatitis B, Measles, Polio and Diphteria show % of *vaccination* coverage, not incidence  
Further information on what these columns represent is explained on the Kaggle page under Data sources:  
[Kaggle data sources](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/lashagoch/life-expectancy-who-updated/data).

### How are the rows structured?

For example, how many countries are there? How many years?  
And do these explain the number of rows seen?
```{r}
row_explain = c(Countries = 0, Years = 0, Product = 0, Nrows = nrow(Life_Expectancy_Data))
row_explain["Countries"] = length(unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country))
row_explain["Years"] = length(unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Year))
row_explain["Product"] = row_explain["Countries"] * row_explain["Years"]
row_explain
```
As you can see, this seems to indicate that all 179 countries occur for all 16 years to explain the 2864 rows in the dataset.  

Which specific years are included?
```{r}
years = unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Year)
years = years[order(years)]
years
```
So from 2000 to 2015  


However, we will further validate this structure:  
How many countries are present 16 times, so once for each year?
```{r}
sum(table(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country) == 16)
```
This all seems right, so the years and countries are used consistently! 


### What data types are present?
```{r column info}
str(Life_Expectancy_Data)
```
The Economy status developing column contains only ones and zeros, so True and False. 
It is the inverse of the developed column.  
The Country and Region columns contain characters, where Region has 9 possibilies. 
All other columns are integers or numeric. 

### What is the life expectancy distribution?
```{r}
boxplot(Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2000,"Life_expectancy"],
        Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2015,"Life_expectancy"],
        main = "Life expectancy distribution for 2000 and 2015",
        names = c(2000, 2015),
        ylab = "Life expectancy (years)",
        ylim = c(30,90))
```


### How many countries are either developed or developing?
```{r row info} 
develop = c(Developed = 0, Developing =  0, Total = 0)
develop["Developed"] = sum(Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developed == T) / 16
develop["Developing"] = sum(Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developed == F) / 16
develop["Total"] = develop[1] + develop[2]
develop
```

### Are there empty values or NA values?
```{r data info}
empty = c(Empty = 0, NAs = 0)
# how many NAs?
empty["NAs"] = sum(is.na(Life_Expectancy_Data))
empty["Empty"] = sum(Life_Expectancy_Data == "")
empty
```
All together, we now understand the data structure and have seen that it is complete. It is important to keep in mind that each country occurs 16 times, once for each year.

## Visualisation:
Here we will make a shiny application that easily lets the user explore life expectancy over time for a selected country. 

```{r}
ui = page_sidebar(
  title = "Life expectancy over time",
  sidebar = sidebar(
    "This graph allows you to select any country in the dataset and then plot
    its life expectancy over time",
    selectInput("country", "Select a country", choices = unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country))
  ),
  card(
    card_header("Life expectancy over time plot"),
    plotOutput("plot")
  )
)

server = function(input, output){
  output$plot = renderPlot({
    x = Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Country == input$country, "Year"]
    y = Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Country == input$country, "Life_expectancy"]
    plot(
      x,y,
      main = paste("Life expectancy over time for", input$country),
      xlab = "Time (years)",
      ylab = "Life expectancy"
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

```
